record_type_quote:
This replication and extension of DeYoung, Quilty, Peterson and Gray’s (2014) study

aimed to assess the unique variance of each of the 10 aspects of the Big Five personality

traits (DeYoung, Quilty & Peterson, 2007) associated to intelligence and its dimensions.

Personality aspects and intelligence were assessed in a sample of French-Canadian adults

from real-life assessment settings (n = 213).

targets.authors: DeYoung, C. G., Quilty, L. C., Peterson, J. B., & Gray, J. R.
targets.title: Openness to experience, Intellect, and Cognitive Ability.
targets.evidence_quote:
A unique and innovative contribution of DeYoung et al.’s (2014) was the study of

the unique variance of both Openness and Intellect aspects in relation to intelligence and

its facets. The authors sought to test the possibility that Openness, which does not

conceptually encompass intelligence, might not be associated with intelligence after

controlling for its shared variance with Intellect. Sequential regressions indicated that only

Intellect incrementally predicted g and nonverbal intelligence, while both Intellect and

Openness contributed incrementally to the prediction of verbal intelligence.

       The present study sought to replicate these findings because of their relevance in

the study of the association between intelligence and personality. This study also aimed to

extend the original study’s methodology by computing the independent associations

between aspects from all five personality traits, as opposed to only Openness to Experience,

and intelligence (g, verbal, nonverbal).
targets.outcome_quote:
In conclusion, despite these limitations and significant methodological differences,

our results supported the principal conclusions of DeYoung et al.’s (2014) study.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The conclusion gives an overall supportive verdict despite differences in secondary correlations and methods.

reasoning: Independent French-Canadian assessment sample retests DeYoung et al. (2014). Overall conclusion explicitly supports the principal original conclusions.
